paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce delivery in 2027?
Discussion document for the board, January 2027
Parcelbird
Board (two founders, two investors)
Board confidential. Synthetic benchmark data: company and figures are fictional

slides.title: Key questions

paragraphs.text: Key questions
Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, in 2027, while keeping 12 months of runway on its $12.0M of cash?
Is quick commerce a market a regional operator can make money in?
Can a Parcelbird dark store make money on each order within 18 months?
Can Parcelbird fund the launch and keep 12 months of runway?
Is the software business a better use of the same cash?
What should the board approve, and what would change the answer?
Decision maker
Success criteria
Timing
Out of scope
Board of Parcelbird (two founders, two investors): approve or reject the launch

Positive profit per order on evidence Parcelbird has, not only on plan inputs; Funded within today's $12.0M of cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; A path to company profitability within the current cash
Board meeting, January 2027
Cities beyond Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City; Raising a new funding round; Buying an existing operator

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: its stores would lose money on every order and break the runway rule; grow the software business instead
Quick commerce is booming, but its operators lose money on every order
–	US sales nearly tripled from 2022 to 2025, yet Zipcart lost $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 an order
A Parcelbird store would lose about $6 an order at the benchmark of 14 sites
–	The plan's profit rests on order value and rider productivity above any site
–	Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three
The launch breaks the cash rule: Parcelbird would be at least $1.9M short at month 18
–	Nine stores at benchmark economics would lose about $18M a year
–	A one-store pilot would cost about $2.6M to confirm a loss
The software business can reach breakeven in early 2029 within today's cash
–	Cash bottoms out at about $5.4M at end-2028; the runway rule holds at 40% growth, not at 30%
Approve software first and sell grocers store-based fast delivery
–	Four gates, led by ARR growth of at least 40%, from mid-2027
–	Reopen own delivery only if a customer site makes money after its fixed costs
